section_title: Spring MVC, REST, Security and JPA

questions.question: How does @Version prevent lost updates, and what happens when two transactions update the same row?
questions.answer: A versioned entity carries a value representing the row version it was loaded from. An update checks that version in its database predicate and advances it on success. If another transaction already changed the row, the stale update affects no matching row and the persistence provider reports an optimistic-lock conflict, often at flush or commit. JPA exposes OptimisticLockException; Spring exception translation can expose an optimistic-locking DataAccessException subtype. I would retry only with a fresh transaction and a freshly loaded state, reapplying a valid business operation. Blindly replaying the stale entity can overwrite the user's intent. This detects conflicting writes; it does not serialize every business decision automatically.

followups.q: Does the exception always appear on save?
followups.a: No. SQL may execute during flush or transaction commit, outside the apparent save call.

followups.q: Do bulk updates automatically honor entity version checks?
followups.a: Do not assume so. Bulk DML bypasses normal managed-entity updates; explicitly design version checks and persistence-context synchronization.

questions.trap: Catching the conflict and retrying in the same failed transaction with the same stale entity.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; round and frequency are estimates.

questions.question: Why might a checked exception leave a Spring transaction committed when you expected rollback?
questions.answer: With the default declarative rollback rules, an escaping RuntimeException or Error triggers rollback, while a checked exception does not automatically do so. I would inspect the configured rules and the exception that actually crosses the transactional proxy boundary. A rollbackFor rule can express the intended checked-exception policy. Catching and swallowing a failure inside the method may make the interceptor see a normal return, though lower layers may already have marked the transaction rollback-only. I would keep exception handling aligned with the transaction boundary and test the resulting database state. Annotation presence alone does not prove interception or rollback occurred.

followups.q: What can rollback-only cause at outer commit?
followups.a: An UnexpectedRollbackException can signal that a shared transaction could not commit despite the outer method returning normally.

followups.q: Should every failure use REQUIRES_NEW?
followups.a: No. It creates a different transaction boundary and may break the required atomicity; use it only for a deliberate independent operation.

questions.trap: Treating every Java exception as equivalent under default Spring rollback rules.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; imperative transaction defaults assumed.

questions.question: An endpoint returns twenty orders but executes many more than twenty queries. How do you diagnose and fix it?
questions.answer: I would correlate SQL with the endpoint and inspect which association access triggers additional selects. Loading a page of orders and then lazily reading each customer's details can create an N+1 pattern. I choose a fetch plan for the use case: a projection, entity graph, fetch join or batch fetching can reduce round trips. Making every relationship eager is not a universal repair and can still produce multiple queries or huge object graphs. Collection fetch joins combined with pagination need special care because joined rows multiply parent records. I would assert both returned results and query behavior with realistic cardinality rather than optimize only a tiny fixture.

followups.q: Why not serialize entities directly?
followups.a: Serialization can traverse relationships, trigger unexpected queries and expose fields. Explicit response DTOs make the query and API contract clearer.

followups.q: Does a cache hide the underlying issue?
followups.a: It can hide it in a warm test while cold requests still suffer. Measure cold and realistic steady-state behavior.

questions.trap: Setting every association to EAGER and assuming N+1 is impossible.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern. Reported in user-provided interview notes, item 6.1 (company not recorded).

questions.question: How would you make validation and business failures consistent across REST controllers?
questions.answer: I would define an error representation with a stable machine-readable code, appropriate HTTP status, safe message and correlation identifier. Controller advice can map relevant MVC exceptions into that contract, while request validation handles malformed or invalid input at the boundary. Business conflicts and unavailable dependencies deserve different responses from validation failures. I avoid returning stack traces, SQL text or secrets to callers. Failures in the security filter chain may occur before controller handling, so authentication entry points and access-denied handlers need compatible responses. Tests should assert status, body and sensitive-data exclusion, including unknown failures that must not be converted into successful responses.

followups.q: Why not return HTTP 200 for all errors?
followups.a: It misleads clients, caches and monitoring; the transport status should reflect the contract's outcome.

followups.q: Is a retry safe for every 500 response?
followups.a: No. A write might already have committed. Clients need operation-specific idempotency and outcome reconciliation.

questions.trap: Assuming controller advice catches every failure in servlet filters and authentication processing.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern.

questions.question: What does @Transactional(readOnly=true) actually promise, and can it prevent every write?
questions.answer: Read-only is a transaction attribute whose effect depends on the transaction manager, persistence provider, driver and database configuration. It can influence connection settings and Hibernate flushing or dirty-checking behavior, but it is not a portable authorization barrier against all writes. I would verify the actual stack's behavior instead of claiming the annotation universally rejects update SQL. A truly read-only database role or an enforced database transaction mode provides a different guarantee. My resume reports read-only transaction management and fewer failures, but the exact cause needs [[HARSH TO FILL: transaction manager, original failure, fix and measurement]]. I would explain that mechanism rather than attribute the improvement to an annotation alone.

followups.q: Can an inner read-only method change an existing transaction?
followups.a: When joining an existing transaction, its effective characteristics are controlled by that existing boundary; do not assume a nested annotation reconfigures it.

followups.q: Does read-only automatically route to a replica?
followups.a: No. Routing requires configured infrastructure and a consistency policy.

questions.trap: Claiming the annotation is a universal database write prohibition.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; resume details intentionally left as placeholders.

questions.question: Trace an HTTP request through Spring MVC from the servlet container to a controller method.
questions.answer: The servlet container receives the request and invokes the configured filter chain before it reaches the DispatcherServlet. The DispatcherServlet consults handler mappings to find a controller method, then a handler adapter invokes it with arguments resolved from the request. Message converters or other argument resolvers turn input into Java values, and a return-value handler writes the response. Exceptions can be handled by MVC resolvers, while security failures may happen earlier in filters. I trace the exact stage before debugging controller code, because malformed input, authorization rejection and serialization failure have different owners and diagnostics.

followups.q: Does every request reach the controller?
followups.a: No. Filters, handler mapping, argument resolution or exception processing can stop it earlier.

followups.q: Where does JSON become a Java request object?
followups.a: Typically through an HttpMessageConverter selected for the handler argument and media type.

questions.trap: Starting investigation at the controller even when a filter or argument resolver rejected the request.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; round, frequency and level are estimates.

questions.question: What are HandlerMapping and HandlerAdapter responsible for in Spring MVC?
questions.answer: A HandlerMapping identifies which handler should process the current request, using information such as path, HTTP method, parameters and headers. A HandlerAdapter knows how to invoke the selected handler type and interpret its arguments and return value. Separating selection from invocation lets MVC support controller methods and other handler forms through shared dispatch infrastructure. If a route returns 404 or a method is not invoked, I check the mapping conditions and registered handler rather than assuming the controller body is at fault. I also verify the effective servlet path and proxy routing because the application may receive a different path than the client sent.

followups.q: Does HandlerMapping serialize the response?
followups.a: No. Return-value handling and message conversion perform response processing.

followups.q: Can two methods map the same path?
followups.a: They need distinguishing conditions or MVC can report an ambiguous mapping.

questions.trap: Treating URL matching, method invocation and response serialization as one controller operation.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; round, frequency and level are estimates.

questions.question: How do servlet filters differ from Spring MVC HandlerInterceptors?
questions.answer: A servlet filter runs in the container's request chain before and after servlet processing, so it can apply to requests that never map to an MVC handler and can wrap request or response objects. A HandlerInterceptor belongs to MVC and runs around a selected handler, with access to handler-specific information. Spring Security normally enforces its web security through filters, before controller interception. I choose a filter for cross-servlet concerns and an interceptor for MVC handler concerns, but avoid using either as a substitute for authorization rules in the security configuration. Ordering and async dispatch behavior depend on registration and execution mode, so I test the actual request path.

followups.q: Can an interceptor protect a request with no MVC handler?
followups.a: No. It is tied to MVC handler processing; a filter can run earlier.

followups.q: Where should access control live?
followups.a: In the security configuration and method policy appropriate to the resource, not an ad hoc logging interceptor.

questions.trap: Calling filters and interceptors interchangeable request hooks and overlooking security's earlier filter chain.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; round, frequency and level are estimates.

questions.question: How does Spring Security decide which SecurityFilterChain handles a request?
questions.answer: The security proxy examines configured SecurityFilterChain matchers and selects the first matching chain according to its ordering and matching rules. Each chain has its own filters and authorization configuration, so a request that matches an unintended broad chain may get a different policy or no expected authentication mechanism. I list the matchers from narrow to broad where appropriate, ensure there is an intentional fallback, and test representative paths, methods and dispatcher routes. The chain matcher decides which security configuration applies; authorization rules inside that chain decide whether the authenticated request may proceed. Those are two separate selection stages. [VERIFY: SecurityFilterChain ordering and matcher behavior against the selected Spring Security 6 minor version]

followups.q: Does authorization configuration choose among chains?
followups.a: No. Chain matching selects the chain first; that chain then applies its own authorization rules.

followups.q: Why include a fallback chain?
followups.a: To define behavior for paths not captured by narrower chains rather than leaving security coverage accidental.

questions.trap: Assuming all configured chains merge their filters and rules for every request.

questions.notes: Unverified pattern; version-sensitive chain semantics are marked for verification; round, frequency and level are estimates.

questions.question: Why does filter order matter in a Spring Security chain?
questions.answer: Filters transform or inspect request state in sequence, so a downstream filter may depend on authentication, context or request wrapping established earlier. An exception handler also needs to surround the component whose failure it is expected to translate. Placing a custom filter at an arbitrary position can cause missing principal data, duplicate processing or an exception that bypasses the intended response handler. I first state what the filter consumes and produces, then place it relative to the relevant framework filter using the supported configuration API. Tests should exercise both successful and rejected requests and confirm exactly one expected response, not merely assert that the filter bean exists. [VERIFY: supported custom-filter placement API for the selected Spring Security 6 minor version]

followups.q: Can a filter order fix a wrong chain matcher?
followups.a: No. The request must first select the intended chain.

followups.q: What is a useful test assertion?
followups.a: Verify the response, authentication state and whether later filters or the controller were reached.

questions.trap: Adding a filter without identifying its prerequisites, ordering contract or duplicate-dispatch behavior.

questions.notes: Unverified pattern; exact placement API is version-sensitive and marked for verification; round, frequency and level are estimates.

questions.question: Explain the difference between authentication and authorization in a request pipeline.
questions.answer: Authentication establishes an identity or principal from the request's credentials according to the configured mechanism. Authorization evaluates whether that principal, with its granted authorities and relevant resource context, may perform the requested action. A request can authenticate successfully and still be forbidden from accessing a particular record. I keep the distinction visible in policy and response handling: unauthenticated access generally invokes an authentication entry point, while an authenticated but disallowed request is handled as access denied. Resource ownership checks may require domain data beyond a URL role matcher. Tests should cover missing identity, insufficient authority and permitted access separately.

followups.q: Can a valid login grant access to every object?
followups.a: No. Authorization must still check the requested action and resource scope.

followups.q: What does HTTP 403 usually represent?
followups.a: An authenticated or otherwise identified request lacks permission, though exact response policy is configurable.

questions.trap: Treating successful credential validation as sufficient authorization for every endpoint and record.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; round, frequency and level are estimates; detailed OAuth protocols remain in S11.

questions.question: What information does SecurityContext hold, and how should request code access it safely?
questions.answer: SecurityContext holds the current Authentication for the execution context managed by Spring Security. That Authentication can describe the principal and its granted authorities, but its exact representation depends on the authentication mechanism. Request code should obtain identity through a clear security boundary, preferably passing the needed domain identity into application operations rather than scattering static context lookups. The security framework manages context persistence and cleanup around web processing; application code must not retain request authentication as mutable global state. For work that outlives the request, define an explicit identity and authorization policy rather than assuming the original request context remains valid.

followups.q: Should a service store Authentication in a singleton field?
followups.a: No. That risks leaking one request's identity into another operation.

followups.q: Does the context itself prove a resource is authorized?
followups.a: No. The application still enforces action and resource-level policy.

questions.trap: Treating the current security context as a globally stable user identity available for arbitrary later work.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; async identity propagation belongs to S05; round, frequency and level are estimates.

questions.question: What threat does CSRF protection address, and when should an API keep it enabled?
questions.answer: Cross-site request forgery abuses a browser's tendency to attach ambient credentials, such as a session cookie, to a request initiated from another site. A CSRF token or an equivalent defense requires the request to carry evidence an attacker cannot obtain merely by causing the browser to send a cookie. Browser-facing applications using cookie authentication generally need a deliberate CSRF strategy, including state-changing requests. Disabling protection because an endpoint returns JSON is not enough; the credential transport and browser behavior matter. A service using non-ambient credentials may have a different threat model, which I document and test instead of applying a blanket API rule.

followups.q: Does JSON content type alone prevent CSRF?
followups.a: No. Evaluate browser credential behavior and the endpoint's accepted request forms.

followups.q: Should every API disable CSRF?
followups.a: No. Decide from the authentication mechanism and browser threat model.

questions.trap: Disabling CSRF solely because the application calls itself REST or returns JSON.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; detailed token protocol and authentication standards remain outside this section; round, frequency and level are estimates.

questions.question: What is CORS, and why is it not a server-side authorization mechanism?
questions.answer: Cross-origin resource sharing is a browser-enforced policy in which a server communicates which origins and request characteristics a browser may allow for a web page. A preflight request can ask permission before the browser sends certain actual requests. CORS does not stop a non-browser client from calling the endpoint and does not decide whether the caller is authenticated or authorized. I configure a narrow origin and method policy, handle credentialed requests deliberately, and ensure the security chain permits preflight processing without opening application data. Tests should inspect the response headers for both preflight and actual requests and separately exercise authorization. [VERIFY: Spring Security CORS behavior and credential constraints for the selected Spring Security 6 minor version]

followups.q: Does CORS block curl or a backend client?
followups.a: No. It is enforced by browsers, not a general network access control.

followups.q: Can wildcard origins be combined freely with credentials?
followups.a: Do not assume so; verify the protocol and framework constraints for the configured response.

questions.trap: Using CORS as a substitute for authentication, authorization or network policy.

questions.question: When should an AuthenticationEntryPoint handle a failure instead of an AccessDeniedHandler?
questions.answer: An AuthenticationEntryPoint starts or reports an authentication challenge when the request cannot proceed because a valid Authentication is absent or unacceptable. An AccessDeniedHandler handles a request that has an established authentication but lacks permission under the policy. These failures may occur in the security filter chain before MVC controller advice can see them, so an API that wants consistent JSON errors must configure both security handlers as needed. I keep response status and body safe and stable, and test unauthenticated and insufficient-authority cases independently. Returning a login redirect from a machine API or a controller-formatted body from a filter failure can violate the client's contract.

followups.q: Will @ControllerAdvice always catch access denial?
followups.a: No. Filter-chain failures can occur before controller dispatch.

followups.q: Should both handlers return identical status codes?
followups.a: Use the API contract and security semantics consistently; do not collapse distinct failures accidentally.

questions.trap: Routing every security failure through controller advice and assuming MVC owns filter exceptions.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; round, frequency and level are estimates.

questions.question: What does stateless security configuration mean, and what must still be handled per request?
questions.answer: A stateless policy means the server does not rely on an HTTP session to retain authentication between requests; each request must present whatever credential the configured mechanism requires. It does not mean the application has no state, that all requests are trustworthy, or that authorization can be skipped. The server must still validate credentials, establish a request Authentication, apply access rules and handle revocation or expiry according to the chosen security design. CSRF decisions depend on whether credentials are ambient in the browser, not merely on a stateless label. I test missing, malformed and valid credentials and verify the session behavior actually configured.

followups.q: Does stateless mean no server-side data anywhere?
followups.a: No. It describes the authentication/session policy, not all application persistence.

followups.q: Does stateless remove authorization checks?
followups.a: No. Each request still needs the policy appropriate to its identity and resource.

questions.trap: Treating stateless configuration as proof that credentials are safe or browser CSRF is impossible.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; no OAuth/JWT protocol mechanics are covered here; round, frequency and level are estimates.

questions.question: How can method-level authorization complement URL-based request rules?
questions.answer: URL rules protect the web entry point, while method security can express authorization close to an application operation that may be called through more than one route. A method policy can check a role or a domain-specific condition, but it should not be the only protection if other entry paths bypass that method boundary. Spring method security is applied through framework interception, so invocation path and proxy constraints matter; self-invocation or manual construction can bypass expected advice. I keep authorization decisions testable and avoid embedding complex database queries in unreadable expressions. Tests should call through the configured boundary and verify both allowed and denied cases. [VERIFY: method-security enablement and interception semantics for the selected Spring Security 6 minor version]

followups.q: Does method security replace HTTP authorization rules?
followups.a: Not necessarily; use layered rules appropriate to each entry point and shared application operation.

followups.q: Can internal self-invocation apply the method policy?
followups.a: Proxy-based interception may be bypassed; verify the actual invocation path and configuration.

questions.trap: Assuming an annotation enforces authorization regardless of how the object is created or invoked.

questions.notes: Unverified pattern; GAP follows the supplied Spring proxy readiness assessment; version-specific enablement is marked for verification.

questions.question: Why might an exception thrown by a custom security filter bypass MVC exception handling?
questions.answer: A security filter executes in the servlet filter chain, which surrounds DispatcherServlet processing. If it throws before the request enters MVC, controller advice and MVC exception resolvers have not yet become the handler for that failure. Security's exception translation component handles only failures that occur within its relevant chain boundary and depends on correct filter placement. I decide whether a filter should reject directly through a security handler or pass a structured failure to a later application layer. The test should send an HTTP request through the real filter chain and assert the response; directly invoking the filter method does not verify surrounding translation behavior. [VERIFY: Spring Security exception translation filter ordering for the selected Spring Security 6 minor version]

followups.q: Can controller advice handle an exception before servlet dispatch?
followups.a: No; it is part of MVC handling after the DispatcherServlet selects that path.

followups.q: How do you test translation?
followups.a: Exercise the configured web chain and assert status, body and whether the controller ran.

questions.trap: Assuming an exception class alone determines which handler catches it, regardless of where it is thrown.
verify: [VERIFY: Spring Security exception translation filter ordering for the selected Spring Security 6 minor version]
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; filter ordering detail is marked for verification; round, frequency and level are estimates.

questions.question: Why can the order of request authorization matchers change which rule applies?
questions.answer: Authorization rules are evaluated against the request using the configured matcher sequence, so a broad rule placed before a narrower rule can capture a path that was meant to receive a more specific policy. I order rules deliberately, put exact public or restricted cases where they are unambiguous, and finish with a deny-by-default or otherwise intentional fallback. Chain selection happens earlier and is a separate concern. I test overlapping paths, HTTP methods, trailing path variants and unmatched requests through the real security setup. A review should verify effective policy, not just that every endpoint name appears somewhere in the configuration. [VERIFY: authorization matcher evaluation order for the selected Spring Security 6 minor version]

followups.q: Does a rule in one SecurityFilterChain apply to another?
followups.a: No. The request first selects a chain; rules are evaluated within the selected chain.

followups.q: What is a useful unmatched-path test?
followups.a: Assert the intended fallback response for a path not covered by explicit rules.

questions.trap: Placing a permit-all pattern broadly and assuming a later restrictive rule will override it.

questions.notes: Unverified pattern; matcher semantics are marked for version verification; round, frequency and level are estimates.

questions.question: How does Spring MVC turn a JSON request body into a controller parameter?
questions.answer: For a request-body argument, MVC selects an HttpMessageConverter using the declared Java type and request media type, then asks that converter to read the body. A JSON converter typically delegates parsing and object mapping to its configured library. Unsupported content types, malformed syntax and a structurally invalid object are different failure cases and can produce different exceptions or status mappings. I define the accepted media types, validate the resulting object and return a stable client error contract. I test actual HTTP requests with correct, missing and unsupported Content-Type headers, because constructing a controller argument directly bypasses converter selection and body parsing.

followups.q: Does @RequestBody validate fields automatically?
followups.a: Binding creates the object; validation requires the applicable validation trigger and constraints.

followups.q: What if the Content-Type is unsupported?
followups.a: MVC can reject the request before invoking the controller; map that error deliberately.

questions.trap: Treating JSON parsing, bean validation and business validation as one automatic step.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; converter implementation depends on the configured stack; round, frequency and level are estimates.

questions.question: When does @ModelAttribute bind request parameters, and how does that differ from @RequestBody?
questions.answer: @ModelAttribute binds request parameters and other eligible web data onto an object through MVC's data-binding process, commonly for form-style submissions or query parameters. @RequestBody instead reads the request body through an HttpMessageConverter, for example mapping JSON into a request DTO. The source and conversion rules differ, so I choose the annotation based on the HTTP contract rather than the shape of the Java class. For either path, I constrain writable fields and validate the result before business processing. Tests should send representative encoded parameters or a body, because direct method calls skip the binding behavior that can expose type-conversion and missing-field errors.

followups.q: Does @ModelAttribute mean JSON parsing?
followups.a: Not by default; JSON request bodies normally use the request-body converter path.

followups.q: Can both forms require validation?
followups.a: Yes. Apply the appropriate validation trigger and inspect binding errors.

questions.trap: Assuming a Java DTO determines whether MVC reads query/form parameters or a serialized body.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; round, frequency and level are estimates.

questions.question: How can broad MVC data binding create a mass-assignment risk?
questions.answer: If a request binds directly onto a persistence or domain object with writable fields the caller should not control, an attacker may submit extra properties such as ownership, status or administrative flags. Binding can then mutate more state than the endpoint intended. I use dedicated request DTOs that expose only accepted inputs, validate them, and map allowed values into domain operations. Authorization still checks whether the caller may perform that operation; hiding a field from the form is not a security control. Tests should submit unexpected properties and verify protected state remains unchanged, including nested objects and update endpoints.

followups.q: Does validation alone prevent mass assignment?
followups.a: Not if the field is bindable and no constraint rejects the supplied value; limit the input shape.

followups.q: Should an entity be the public request schema?
followups.a: Usually not; persistence fields and API write permissions have different lifecycles.

questions.trap: Relying on clients to omit sensitive entity properties instead of defining a narrow accepted request model.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; round, frequency and level are estimates.

questions.question: What does @Valid trigger on a controller argument, and where do validation errors go?
questions.answer: When validation is configured and the argument has applicable constraints, @Valid asks the MVC argument-processing path to validate the bound object. For a request body, constraint failures typically prevent normal controller execution and are represented as a method-argument validation exception; form binding can instead expose binding and validation errors through a BindingResult parameter when positioned appropriately. I normalize these outcomes into the API's safe validation response and avoid returning internal constraint details that reveal implementation. I test missing fields, malformed types and constraint violations over HTTP, because a unit test that creates an invalid object does not prove MVC invokes validation or maps the response correctly. [VERIFY: Spring MVC validation exception types for the selected Spring Framework 6 minor version]

followups.q: Does @Valid create constraints?
followups.a: No. It triggers evaluation of constraints declared on the object and its validated graph.

followups.q: Can a controller run after validation errors?
followups.a: Depending on the binding path and BindingResult usage, errors may be exposed rather than thrown; define the contract.

questions.trap: Assuming @Valid rejects every invalid request even when validation infrastructure or constraints are absent.
verify: [VERIFY: Spring MVC validation exception types for the selected Spring Framework 6 minor version]
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; exact exception type can vary with MVC method signature and release; round, frequency and level are estimates.

questions.question: When might validation groups be useful, and why can separate request DTOs be clearer?
questions.answer: Validation groups let one object apply different constraint sets for distinct operations, such as creation and partial update. They can reduce duplication when the same data structure genuinely has a stable shared meaning. However, a DTO carrying many groups can become difficult to understand, and update semantics often differ enough that separate request types are clearer. I choose based on whether the accepted fields and invariants are actually shared, then test each endpoint's group selection and nested validation. Groups do not implement authorization or define which omitted fields remain unchanged; those semantics belong to the request and domain contract. Version-sensitive integration details should be checked against the chosen validation provider. [VERIFY: validation group integration for the selected Spring Framework and Bean Validation provider versions]

followups.q: Do groups decide which fields the client may modify?
followups.a: No. The DTO shape and mapping define writable input; groups only select constraints.

followups.q: When prefer separate DTOs?
followups.a: When operations have materially different fields, meanings or invariants.

questions.trap: Using validation groups to disguise incompatible create and update models as one request contract.
verify: [VERIFY: validation group integration for the selected Spring Framework and Bean Validation provider versions]
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; provider integration is marked for verification; round, frequency and level are estimates.

questions.question: What is the purpose of BindingResult next to a validated MVC argument?
questions.answer: BindingResult gives a controller access to binding and validation errors for the associated model attribute, allowing it to choose a response instead of relying solely on an exception path. Its position relative to the bound argument matters: it must be associated with the parameter whose errors it represents. For a JSON API, central exception handling may produce a more consistent contract than handling each result manually, while a form workflow may need to redisplay field errors. I do not ignore a non-empty result and continue with a partially bound object. Tests should cover both valid and invalid submissions and confirm which layer formats the response.

followups.q: Can BindingResult belong to any earlier controller argument?
followups.a: It is associated with the relevant bindable argument and must be placed according to MVC's method-argument contract.

followups.q: Should business logic run with binding errors?
followups.a: No, unless the operation explicitly handles them; reject or render the invalid input deliberately.

questions.trap: Accepting partially bound data because validation errors were captured instead of thrown.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; round, frequency and level are estimates.

questions.question: How do you model an optional query parameter without confusing absence and an empty value?
questions.answer: I define whether omission means use a default, leave a field unchanged, or reject the request, and distinguish that from an explicitly empty string. MVC can bind query parameters to typed values and report conversion failures before the controller runs. A nullable wrapper or an explicit optional representation can preserve absence when it has real domain meaning; primitive defaults can erase that distinction. I document the contract in the API schema and test omitted, empty, malformed and valid values over HTTP. Defaults should be stable and should not silently broaden a query or change authorization scope.

followups.q: Can a primitive distinguish missing from zero?
followups.a: Not by itself; choose a representation that preserves absence if it matters.

followups.q: Where should invalid numeric input fail?
followups.a: At request binding with a consistent client-error response, before domain logic runs.

questions.trap: Using a default that makes an omitted filter mean 'return every record' without considering the contract or access boundary.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; round, frequency and level are estimates.

questions.question: What happens when a path variable cannot be converted to the controller parameter type?
questions.answer: MVC resolves the path segment and converts its text to the declared Java parameter type before invoking the controller. If conversion fails, handler argument resolution raises an exception and the method body is not reached. I distinguish that malformed identifier from a syntactically valid identifier for which no resource exists, because the API may assign different status and error codes. I use a stable value type when identifiers have domain meaning, centralize safe error mapping and test malformed, absent and unknown-resource cases through HTTP. A route that is too permissive can also make two mappings ambiguous.

followups.q: Does failed conversion mean the resource was not found?
followups.a: No. The controller may never run; the input could not be parsed as its declared identifier type.

followups.q: Should parsing errors expose stack traces?
followups.a: No. Return a safe client error with a stable contract.

questions.trap: Mapping every conversion failure to a database not-found result even though no lookup occurred.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; round, frequency and level are estimates.

questions.question: How would you make enum and date query parameters predictable for API clients?
questions.answer: I define a documented external representation rather than exposing an incidental Java enum name or locale-dependent date format. MVC's conversion service converts request text into the declared type, and unsupported values should fail before business processing with a clear client response. If public enum values may evolve, I map stable API values to internal constants instead of renaming the Java field and breaking clients. Dates should specify an unambiguous format and timezone semantics. I test accepted, boundary and invalid forms, including case behavior, and ensure generated API documentation matches the converter behavior actually configured.

followups.q: Can renaming a Java enum constant break clients?
followups.a: Yes, if its name is the serialized request contract; use an explicit stable external mapping.

followups.q: Should dates rely on server locale?
followups.a: No. Specify an unambiguous wire format and timezone meaning.

questions.trap: Treating a Java type's default string conversion as a durable public API contract.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; exact conversion behavior depends on registered converters; round, frequency and level are estimates.

questions.question: When does returning ResponseEntity help, and when is a plain DTO sufficient?
questions.answer: A plain DTO is enough when the controller's response body and default success status express the contract. ResponseEntity is useful when the operation must select a status, headers or conditional response at runtime, such as returning a resource location after creation or a no-content response. I keep transport decisions at the controller boundary and avoid wrapping every response in a generic envelope merely to carry a status already represented by HTTP. The body remains an explicit response model, not a persistence entity. Tests should assert status, important headers and body shape together so clients see the complete contract.

followups.q: Does ResponseEntity make a response RESTful automatically?
followups.a: No. The status, headers and body still need to fit the resource contract.

followups.q: When is a bodyless response appropriate?
followups.a: When the operation contract has no representation to return, such as a successful delete or update defined that way.

questions.trap: Using ResponseEntity everywhere without adding meaningful transport control, or returning entities directly because the wrapper can hold them.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; round, frequency and level are estimates.

questions.question: How should an API distinguish PUT replacement from PATCH partial modification?
questions.answer: PUT conventionally represents replacing the target resource's state with the supplied representation, while PATCH applies a defined partial-change document or operation. The API must specify what omitted, null and empty fields mean; otherwise a mapper can accidentally clear values or preserve fields unpredictably. I use separate request models or an explicit patch format so the operation's semantics are visible, validate permitted changes, and check resource authorization. I test repeated and partial requests against the documented result. Neither verb should be chosen solely because the client library makes one easier; the contract must explain what state transition it requests.

followups.q: Does null always mean clear a field in PATCH?
followups.a: Only if the chosen patch format and API contract define it that way.

followups.q: Can a mapper safely copy every DTO field?
followups.a: Not without an explicit allowlist and a clear policy for absent values.

questions.trap: Implementing PATCH as an ambiguous nullable DTO copy and losing the distinction between omitted and explicitly cleared fields.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; round, frequency and level are estimates.

questions.question: How do you choose between 400, 401, 403, 404 and 409 for an API failure?
questions.answer: I map the status to the failure's meaning in the API contract: malformed or unacceptable input is generally a client error; missing or invalid authentication requires the configured authentication response; an authenticated caller without permission is forbidden; an unavailable resource may be not found; and a state conflict can use a conflict response. There can be deliberate security reasons not to reveal whether a protected resource exists, so the contract may choose a consistent not-found result. I keep machine-readable error codes stable and test the security filter and controller paths separately because they are handled at different layers.

followups.q: Is 401 the same as forbidden?
followups.a: No. It represents an authentication challenge or failure, while forbidden reflects denied access under policy.

followups.q: Can a protected missing resource return 404?
followups.a: Yes, if the documented security policy avoids disclosing its existence.

questions.trap: Returning one generic 200 or 500 for all failures and losing protocol meaning for clients and monitoring.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; status choices must follow the API's security and resource contract; round, frequency and level are estimates.

questions.question: How does HTTP content negotiation affect Spring MVC response selection?
questions.answer: The client's Accept header expresses response media types it can consume, while the request Content-Type describes the body format it sent. MVC selects a compatible handler return converter and representation based on the declared mappings and configured converters. A request can therefore fail even when the controller method itself is correct, for example when no acceptable response type exists. I document supported media types, avoid using Content-Type to describe the desired response, and test JSON and unsupported Accept values over HTTP. Content negotiation does not version the data model by itself; a compatible representation still needs an intentional schema evolution policy.

followups.q: Which header describes the request body?
followups.a: Content-Type describes the media type of the representation sent by the client.

followups.q: Which header expresses acceptable response formats?
followups.a: Accept communicates the response media types the client can consume.

questions.trap: Swapping Accept and Content-Type or assuming a converter always returns JSON regardless of negotiation.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; response details depend on configured converters; round, frequency and level are estimates.

questions.question: What is the difference between produces and consumes on an MVC mapping?
questions.answer: A consumes condition constrains the media type of the request representation the handler accepts, which is normally compared with Content-Type. A produces condition constrains the response representation the handler can return, typically in relation to Accept negotiation. These conditions participate in handler selection, so a path and method can exist but still fail to match because the client's headers are incompatible. I use them to make endpoint contracts explicit where media types matter and return consistent errors for unsupported combinations. I test the mapping with both matching and mismatching headers rather than checking only the controller's path annotation.

followups.q: Can consumes describe the response?
followups.a: No. It concerns accepted request representations; produces concerns response representations.

followups.q: Can header mismatch look like a missing route?
followups.a: Yes, handler selection considers mapping conditions in addition to path and method.

questions.trap: Assuming path and HTTP verb alone determine whether an MVC handler matches.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; round, frequency and level are estimates.

questions.question: How does @ControllerAdvice centralize MVC exception handling, and what are its boundaries?
questions.answer: Controller advice contributes exception handling and other controller-related behavior across selected MVC controllers, allowing one place to map expected exceptions into a consistent response. Scope can be narrowed by package, annotation or controller type, which is useful when APIs have different contracts. It participates in MVC exception resolution after request dispatch; it does not automatically catch failures that occur earlier in servlet security filters or outside the web request. I order and scope handlers deliberately so a broad fallback does not swallow a more specific case, and test status, body and header outcomes through MockMvc or an HTTP test appropriate to the application.

followups.q: Can advice handle a filter exception before DispatcherServlet?
followups.a: Not through ordinary MVC exception resolution; configure the relevant filter-chain handler.

followups.q: Why narrow advice scope?
followups.a: Different controller groups may have distinct representations or compatibility contracts.

questions.trap: Assuming controller advice is a global process-wide exception handler for every failure source.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; round, frequency and level are estimates.

questions.question: What problem does a standard problem-details response solve for REST APIs?
questions.answer: A problem-details representation provides a common structure for describing an HTTP error with fields such as a stable type, title, status and instance, while allowing carefully chosen extensions. It helps clients handle errors consistently without parsing framework exception text. The API still owns its error taxonomy, localization, correlation identifiers and sensitive-data policy; adopting a format does not make every exception safe to expose. I map validation, conflict and unexpected failures intentionally and test the serialized media type and fields. Spring's built-in support and exact customization points vary by release, so I verify the selected Framework version before depending on a particular API. [VERIFY: ProblemDetail support and customization APIs for the selected Spring Framework 6 minor version]

followups.q: Does a standard format define business error codes?
followups.a: No. The API must define stable meanings and extensions for its clients.

followups.q: Should exception messages be returned as detail?
followups.a: Only if they are safe and useful; internal messages can expose implementation or sensitive data.

questions.trap: Assuming a standard error object automatically makes raw exception details appropriate for clients.

questions.notes: Unverified pattern; Framework API availability is marked for verification; round, frequency and level are estimates.

questions.question: How do you keep validation error responses stable when Java DTO fields change?
questions.answer: I treat validation output as a public API contract rather than serializing provider exception objects. The response can include a stable field path, application error code and safe explanation, while omitting Java class names, rejected secrets and internal constraint implementation. If DTO properties are renamed, I decide whether external field names change or remain mapped to a stable API name. I normalize ordering when clients or tests depend on deterministic output and avoid promising localized text as a machine key. Contract tests should assert representative field errors and verify that changes to internal classes do not accidentally alter the wire response.

followups.q: Should clients branch on the human message?
followups.a: No. Provide a stable code and treat prose as explanatory text.

followups.q: Can rejected values be echoed back?
followups.a: Avoid echoing credentials, personal data or other sensitive input.

questions.trap: Returning framework validation objects directly and coupling clients to internal provider details.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; round, frequency and level are estimates.

questions.question: Why separate request and response DTOs from JPA entities?
questions.answer: An entity models persistence state and relationships, while an API DTO models what a client may send or receive. Reusing the entity can expose internal fields, allow mass assignment and tie a public contract to schema or fetch behavior. Serialization may also traverse lazy relationships and cause unexpected database access. I map explicitly at the application boundary, validate writable inputs and return stable representations that can evolve independently. The mapping should preserve authorization rules and avoid copying fields clients do not own. Tests verify both allowed fields and the absence of internal data; a DTO is not merely ceremony when these boundaries differ.

followups.q: Does a DTO automatically prevent unauthorized updates?
followups.a: No. Explicit mapping narrows input, while authorization and domain invariants still apply.

followups.q: Can entity serialization trigger queries?
followups.a: Yes, depending on accessed associations and persistence context behavior.

questions.trap: Returning a persistence entity directly and assuming its current fields are a safe, stable public schema.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; round, frequency and level are estimates.

questions.question: What should a successful REST create response communicate to its client?
questions.answer: The response should communicate that the resource was created, identify it in a stable way, and return the representation or location information promised by the API. For a newly created resource, a 201 response with a Location header is a common contract; the body may include the canonical representation if useful. I ensure the location is built from the externally visible resource route rather than an internal host assumption, and avoid exposing generated persistence details unintentionally. Tests assert status, Location and body together, including any validation or conflict path. A successful response should reflect committed application state, not merely that a controller constructed an object.

followups.q: Must a 201 response always include a body?
followups.a: The API can define otherwise; a location or other representation should make the created resource discoverable.

followups.q: Should Location use an internal server hostname?
followups.a: No. Construct it according to the public routing contract and deployment topology.

questions.trap: Returning success before persistence has actually completed or omitting the promised resource identity.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; round, frequency and level are estimates.

questions.question: How do safe and idempotent HTTP methods differ?
questions.answer: Safety means a request is defined not to change the server's resource state; idempotence means repeating the same request has the same intended state effect as performing it once. A safe operation is normally idempotent, but an idempotent operation can change state: PUT may replace a resource and DELETE may remove it once, while repeats leave the intended result unchanged. Logging or metrics can still occur without changing the resource semantics. I use these definitions to make method contracts clear and do not infer side-effect behavior from controller annotations alone.

followups.q: What does safe mean for GET?
followups.a: It is intended to retrieve a representation without requesting a resource-state change.

followups.q: Is DELETE idempotent if a repeated call returns 404?
followups.a: It can be: the intended state after each call is absence, even if response statuses differ.

questions.trap: Saying every idempotent operation is read-only; an idempotent update can change resource state.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; round, frequency and level are estimates.

questions.question: How should an API bound page size and validate client-supplied pagination parameters?
questions.answer: I define a default and maximum page size, reject or cap invalid values consistently, and guard against negative page indexes and integer overflow. An unbounded client request can create expensive database work and large serialized responses. I also whitelist sortable properties rather than passing arbitrary strings into query construction, and document whether pages are zero- or one-based. Tests cover default, maximum, oversized and malformed inputs, including stable error behavior. A size limit protects one dimension only; query shape, authorization scope and result cardinality still need review. The response should communicate pagination metadata without implying a stable snapshot across concurrent changes.

followups.q: Should oversized sizes always be silently capped?
followups.a: Choose and document either rejection or capping; inconsistent behavior surprises clients.

followups.q: Does bounded page size guarantee a cheap query?
followups.a: No. Filters, joins and counts can still be expensive.

questions.trap: Accepting arbitrary page size and sort input because Spring can bind it to Pageable.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; round, frequency and level are estimates.

questions.question: Why should public sort parameters map through an allowlist instead of becoming query property names directly?
questions.answer: A client-facing sort key is part of the API vocabulary, while an entity property is an internal persistence detail. Passing arbitrary client strings directly into sort or query construction can expose fields the API should not reveal, fail at runtime, or create costly query plans. I map a small set of documented public names to known entity paths and allowed directions, reject unknown values, and apply a deterministic tie-breaker where pagination needs stable ordering. This is not a claim that ordinary parameter binding itself executes SQL injection; it is an allowlist and query-contract boundary. Tests cover unknown, nested and disallowed fields.

followups.q: Is binding a sort string automatically SQL injection?
followups.a: Not inherently; the concern is uncontrolled query shape, exposure and provider-specific behavior.

followups.q: Why add a tie-breaker?
followups.a: Equal sort values otherwise can move between pages unpredictably.

questions.trap: Claiming every Pageable sort string is raw SQL, or accepting every internal entity property as public API.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; round, frequency and level are estimates.

questions.question: Why can a servlet filter observe more than one dispatch for what users consider one request?
questions.answer: Servlet processing can involve different dispatcher types, such as an initial request followed by an error or asynchronous dispatch. Whether a filter runs for each depends on its registration's dispatcher-type mapping and, for framework filters, its implementation contract. Logging, metrics or request mutation can therefore happen more than once unless the filter accounts for redispatch. I first inspect the actual container registration and request lifecycle, then test normal, error and async paths if those are supported. I avoid claiming exactly-once execution from a filter name alone; the precise behavior is version and registration sensitive and should be checked against the deployed servlet stack. [VERIFY: servlet filter dispatcher-type behavior for the selected container and Spring Framework 6 minor version]

followups.q: Can an error dispatch invoke filters again?
followups.a: It can when the filter is mapped for that dispatcher type; inspect registration and container behavior.

followups.q: Should a metric count every dispatch as a new client request?
followups.a: Not without defining whether it measures dispatches or logical requests.

questions.trap: Assuming a servlet filter always executes exactly once for a logical HTTP request.

questions.notes: Unverified pattern; container and registration details are marked for verification; round, frequency and level are estimates.

questions.question: What does OncePerRequestFilter's once-per-request wording mean in a servlet application?
questions.answer: OncePerRequestFilter provides a framework convention for avoiding repeated execution during a request's dispatch lifecycle, but its behavior is tied to dispatcher types and its async or error dispatch hooks. The name should not be read as a universal guarantee that the filter runs once across every container dispatch and every registration arrangement. I inspect the implementation defaults and registration mapping for the actual Spring release, then decide whether the filter should run on async or error dispatches. For security, correlation IDs or metrics, that decision affects correctness. Tests should assert observed calls and request attributes through the container-style chain rather than instantiate the filter alone. [VERIFY: OncePerRequestFilter async/error dispatch defaults in the selected Spring Framework 6 minor version]

followups.q: Does the class name settle async behavior?
followups.a: No. Check the filter's dispatch hooks and servlet registration.

followups.q: Should every custom filter run on error dispatch?
followups.a: Only when its responsibility needs to process that dispatch and duplicate effects are controlled.

questions.trap: Treating 'once' as exactly once for the entire network request regardless of dispatch configuration.

questions.question: What can go wrong if a security filter is registered both with the servlet container and inside Spring Security?
questions.answer: A filter that is both auto-registered with the servlet container and inserted into Spring Security's chain can execute twice at different points in the request path. That can duplicate authentication work, consume a request body, emit repeated logs or produce inconsistent context state. I decide which layer owns the filter, disable the unintended registration using the supported configuration, and verify its exact chain position. The relevant debugging evidence is an HTTP trace or invocation counter across the real server, not just the number of filter beans. I also test error and async dispatch if the filter can participate in them. [VERIFY: filter bean servlet auto-registration and disablement mechanism for the selected Boot minor version]

followups.q: Can a bean filter be auto-registered by Boot?
followups.a: Depending on its type and configuration, servlet registration may occur; verify the actual application setup.

followups.q: How do you prove it runs twice?
followups.a: Trace invocations through the running filter chain and distinguish container and security-chain positions.

questions.trap: Assuming a filter bean is only active in Spring Security because it was also added to that chain.

questions.notes: Unverified pattern; Boot registration behavior is marked for selected-version verification; round, frequency and level are estimates.

questions.question: What role does UserDetailsService play, and what does it not define by itself?
questions.answer: UserDetailsService is a contract for loading user data by a username in authentication flows that use that lookup model. It supplies details such as the principal and authorities to the surrounding authentication provider; it does not by itself decide every password check, request authorization rule, account lifecycle or API response. I keep account lookup, credential verification and access policy conceptually separate, and avoid returning sensitive credential material outside the authentication boundary. A custom implementation should handle unknown users consistently with the selected security policy and avoid leaking account existence. I test the configured provider path rather than testing the lookup class alone and claiming end-to-end authentication works.

followups.q: Does UserDetailsService enforce endpoint authorization?
followups.a: No. It supplies user details; request and method policies authorize operations.

followups.q: Does implementing it prove password verification is secure?
followups.a: No. Verify the configured provider and password encoder behavior separately.

questions.trap: Describing UserDetailsService as the entire authentication and authorization system.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; OAuth and identity-protocol details are reserved for S11; round, frequency and level are estimates.

questions.question: Why should an application store encoded passwords rather than reversible encrypted passwords?
questions.answer: A password encoder should use a one-way, deliberately expensive password-hashing scheme with a per-password salt so a database disclosure does not reveal reusable plaintext credentials. Authentication verifies a presented password against the stored encoded value; the application should not decrypt it. Work factor and algorithm choice need maintenance as hardware changes, and migration can use an encoder identifier or rehash-on-success strategy. I never log passwords or compare encoded strings as though random salts make them identical. This is local credential handling, not a replacement for the OAuth, OIDC or federation protocols covered elsewhere. Tests should verify matching and non-matching credentials without storing real secrets. [VERIFY: Spring Security password encoder recommendations for the selected Spring Security 6 minor version]

followups.q: Can the application recover a user's original password?
followups.a: No. A password hash is verified by matching a new encoding process, not decrypted.

followups.q: Should hashes use a fast general-purpose digest?
followups.a: No. Password storage needs a suitable adaptive password-hashing scheme and maintained parameters.

questions.trap: Calling reversible encryption or a fast unsalted digest secure password storage.
verify: [VERIFY: Spring Security password encoder recommendations for the selected Spring Security 6 minor version]
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; current algorithm recommendations are marked for version verification; round, frequency and level are estimates.

questions.question: What is session fixation, and what does session-fixation protection aim to change?
questions.answer: Session fixation is an attack where a victim is induced to authenticate using a session identifier the attacker already knows, allowing the attacker to reuse that identifier after login. Protection changes or invalidates the session identifier when the authentication state changes, according to the chosen session strategy. I verify the effective policy for the application's authentication mechanism and test the session before and after successful login. This control does not replace secure cookie settings, transport protection or authorization checks. Stateless API configurations may not rely on an HTTP session in the same way, so I do not enable session-specific controls without understanding whether sessions are actually used. [VERIFY: Spring Security session-fixation defaults for the selected Spring Security 6 minor version]

followups.q: Does session rotation grant authorization by itself?
followups.a: No. It protects session identity; authorization remains a separate decision.

followups.q: Is this relevant when no HTTP session is used?
followups.a: The classic session-fixation concern is different; verify the actual credential and session model.

questions.trap: Treating session-fixation protection as a general defense for every stateless credential scheme.

questions.question: How should an API team think about security response headers in Spring Security?
questions.answer: Security headers communicate browser-facing protections, such as restrictions on framing or content handling, but their usefulness depends on the clients and content the service actually serves. I review the configured header writers and any reverse-proxy modifications, then test the final response as seen by the browser. A JSON API and an application serving HTML can need different policies, and blindly removing defaults to satisfy one integration may weaken another route. Headers complement input validation, authorization and secure transport; they do not repair those controls. I document intentional exceptions and include them in an HTTP contract test so future configuration changes do not silently remove them. [VERIFY: Spring Security default header set for the selected Spring Security 6 minor version]

followups.q: Do headers replace access control?
followups.a: No. They are defense-in-depth signals and do not authorize a server request.

followups.q: Where should final headers be checked?
followups.a: At the externally observed response, including any gateway or proxy transformations.

questions.trap: Assuming framework defaults match every browser and reverse-proxy deployment without checking the final response.

questions.question: What does a MockMvc security test validate, and when is a running-server test still needed?
questions.answer: A MockMvc test can exercise MVC request mapping, argument binding, configured filters and response handling in a test-managed servlet environment when the relevant application configuration is loaded. It is fast for checking authorization outcomes, validation and error contracts. It may not reproduce a real embedded container, network proxy, TLS termination, deployment path rewriting or every servlet dispatch behavior. I choose the test level based on the failure mode and keep a smaller number of running-server checks for container and deployment integration. A test that manually supplies an authenticated principal also does not prove the production credential verification mechanism.

followups.q: Does with(user) prove password authentication works?
followups.a: No. It supplies a test principal; the actual credential provider needs its own test.

followups.q: When use a running-server test?
followups.a: When container, network, servlet dispatch or deployment integration is part of the contract.

questions.trap: Calling a mock-request test proof of the production network, proxy and credential configuration.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; no tests have been run; round, frequency and level are estimates.

questions.question: How would you review a Spring Security configuration for unintended public endpoints?
questions.answer: I enumerate the routes and security chains, identify which requests each chain matches, and compare every authorization rule with the intended public and protected resource contract. I pay special attention to broad path matchers, alternate HTTP methods, error routes and management endpoints, then verify there is a deliberate fallback for unmatched requests. I test representative allowed and denied cases with both anonymous and authenticated callers, including object-level ownership checks. The review should use the effective configuration after all imports and profiles, not only one SecurityFilterChain declaration. Detailed identity-token protocols are a separate concern; here the focus is route coverage and authorization policy.

followups.q: Is testing only the happy-path endpoint enough?
followups.a: No. Test anonymous, insufficient-authority, alternate-method and unmatched-route behavior.

followups.q: Can one chain cover the full application?
followups.a: It can, but verify its matcher and rules actually cover every intended route.

questions.trap: Reviewing only the named controller routes while ignoring broad matchers, alternate methods or another chain.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; no configuration has been integration-tested; round, frequency and level are estimates.

questions.question: How would you prevent an authenticated caller from accessing another user's record by changing an identifier?
questions.answer: Authentication only identifies the caller; the application must still establish that this caller may access the requested record. I avoid loading an entity by identifier and returning it solely because the caller reached an authenticated endpoint. The service can scope the lookup to the caller's permitted tenant or ownership context, or perform an explicit policy check before exposing or mutating state. I define how unauthorized and nonexistent resources appear in the API to avoid accidental information disclosure. Tests should use two principals and verify that changing an ID cannot cross the authorization boundary, including update and delete operations.

followups.q: Does a random UUID prevent this problem?
followups.a: No. Unpredictable identifiers are not an authorization check.

followups.q: Where can the ownership check live?
followups.a: In a clear application authorization boundary or scoped query, with consistent domain policy.

questions.trap: Assuming authentication or an unguessable database identifier makes resource access authorized.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; no personal implementation is claimed; round, frequency and level are estimates.

questions.question: How do roles and authorities differ in Spring Security policy expressions?
questions.answer: An authority is a granted permission string carried by an Authentication, while a role is commonly treated as a convention for a coarser group of permissions. Spring's role-oriented checks may apply a configured role prefix, whereas authority checks compare the specified authority according to their contract. I choose one vocabulary deliberately and keep naming consistent between user loading, request rules and method policies. A role such as ADMIN should not become a substitute for resource ownership or fine-grained permission checks. Tests should verify the actual authorities loaded for a principal and the policy result, because a prefix mismatch can deny access even when the configuration looks plausible. [VERIFY: role-prefix behavior for the selected Spring Security 6 minor version]

followups.q: Does a role prove ownership of a particular record?
followups.a: No. Record-level authorization needs resource context or a scoped permission.

followups.q: Why can a role check unexpectedly fail?
followups.a: The stored authority and configured role-prefix convention may not match.

questions.trap: Treating roles and arbitrary authorities as interchangeable strings with identical matching semantics.
